claim: The Moon moves about 3.8 cm (1.5 inches) farther from Earth every year because Earth's tidal bulge, carried ahead by Earth's faster spin, tugs the Moon forward into a higher orbit.

beats.caption: 1.5 inches farther every year
beats.vo: Every year it drifts about an inch and a half farther away. We know, because Apollo astronauts left mirrors up there, and we still bounce lasers off them.

beats.caption: Blame the tides
beats.vo: Blame the tides. The Moon raises a bulge in our oceans, but Earth spins so fast the bulge runs ahead of the Moon. That bulge tugs the Moon forward, and a forward tug lifts it into a higher orbit.

beats.caption: 7 feet farther since Apollo 11
beats.vo: That same tug slows Earth's spin, so our days get a tiny bit longer too. And since Apollo 11 landed, the Moon has moved about seven feet farther away. So will we ever lose it? Not in your lifetime.

sources.text: NASA JPL, The Apollo Experiment That Keeps on Giving (July 24, 2019): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/the-apollo-experiment-that-keeps-on-giving/ (3.8 cm per year; tidal bulge pulls the Moon forward and slows Earth's rotation; Apollo 11, 14 and 15 reflectors)

NASA GSFC Eclipse site, Measuring the Moon's Distance (LPI Bulletin 72, 1994): https://eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/SEhelp/ApolloLaser.html (Moon receding about 3.8 cm per year; ocean tides influence the Moon's orbit)
NASA Science, Moon Facts: https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/ (about an inch farther each year; average distance 238,855 miles)
Arithmetic for 'seven feet': 57 years since July 1969 x 3.8 cm = 217 cm = 7.1 ft
